{{short description|Constant relating to close packing of spheres}}
[[File:Hermite constant.svg|thumb|A hexagonal lattice with unit covolume (the area of the quadrilateral is 1). Both arrows are minimum non-zero elements for <math>n-1</math> with length <math display=inline>\lambda_n=\sqrt{\gamma_n}=\sqrt{2/\sqrt{3}}</math>.]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''Hermite constant''', named after [[Charles Hermite]], determines how long a shortest element of a [[lattice (group)|lattice]] in [[Euclidean space]] can be.

The constant <math>\gamma_n</math> for integers <math>n>0</math> is defined as follows.  For a lattice <math>L</math> in Euclidean space <math>\R^n</math> with unit covolume, i.e. <math>\operatorname{vol}(\R^n/L)=1</math>, let <math>\lambda_1(L)</math> denote the least length of a nonzero element of <math>L</math>.  Then <math>\sqrt{\gamma_n}</math> is the maximum of <math>\lambda_1(L)</math> over all such lattices <math>L</math>.

The [[square root]] in the definition of the Hermite constant is a matter of historical convention.

Alternatively, the Hermite constant <math>\gamma_n</math> can be defined as the square of the maximal [[systolic geometry|systole]] of a flat <math>n</math>-dimensional [[torus]] of unit volume.

==Examples==
The Hermite constant is known in dimensions 1–8 and 24. 

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center; width:15cm;"
|-
! scope=row|{{math|''n''}}
| 1
| 2
| 3
| 4
| 5
| 6
| 7
| 8
| 24
|-
! scope=row|{{math|''<math>\gamma_n</math>''}}
| <math>1</math>
| <math>\frac 2 {\sqrt 3}</math>
| <math>\sqrt[3]2</math>
| <math>\sqrt 2</math>
| <math>\sqrt[5]8</math>
|<math>\frac 2 {\sqrt[6]3}</math>
| <math>\sqrt[7]{64}</math>
| <math>2</math>
| <math>4</math>
|}

For <math>n=2</math>, one has <math>\gamma_2=2/\sqrt{3}</math>.  This value is attained by the [[hexagonal lattice]] of the [[Eisenstein integers]], scaled to have a [[Fundamental pair of periods|fundamental parallelogram]] with unit area.<ref>Cassels (1971) p. 36</ref>

==Estimates==
It is known that<ref name=K36>Kitaoka (1993) p. 36</ref>

<math display=block>\gamma_n \le \left( \frac 4 3 \right)^\frac{n-1}{2}.</math>

A stronger estimate due to [[Hans Frederick Blichfeldt]]<ref>{{cite journal | last=Blichfeldt | first=H. F. | authorlink=Hans Frederick Blichfeldt | title=The minimum value of quadratic forms, and the closest packing of spheres | journal=Math. Ann. | volume=101 | pages=605–608 | year=1929 | jfm=55.0721.01 | doi=10.1007/bf01454863| s2cid=123648492 }}</ref> is<ref name=K42>Kitaoka (1993) p. 42</ref>

<math display=block>\gamma_n \le \left( \frac 2 \pi \right)\Gamma\left(2 + \frac n 2\right)^\frac{2}{n},</math>
where <math>\Gamma(x)</math> is the [[gamma function]].
